extracted.intended_audience: researchers writing or responding to NIH/academic grant proposals (applicants, mentors, and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for preparing research grant proposals (especially NIH-style) and for assessing the quality and conduct of peer reviews; emphasizes clarity, audience assumptions, reviewer expertise, and professional tone. Useful for applicants, mentors, and reviewers seeking to improve proposal writing and review practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume reviewers are not narrow experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect assigned reviewers to be expert peers for every application; many reviewers may have only a graduate-student level acquaintance with your topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write your proposal assuming some reviewers are only modestly familiar with the narrow subject matter. Several comments: "many peers who do not work directly in the narrow topic you are proposing to study have essentially a graduate student level acquaintance with your topic"; "Write your proposal accordingly."

rubrics_metrics.name: Make interpretations and background explicit within the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the applicant's job to make interpretations clear rather than relying on reviewers to infer or to know contested background material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are papers pointing in different directions in the literature, explain those differences in the proposal. Quoted guidance: "As a grant applicant, I'm sorry, but it is your job to make your interpretations clear, particularly if you know there are papers pointing in different directions in the literature."

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on reviewers to read external materials (papers/blogs/links)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are not expected to do extensive outside reading of your papers or to follow links you provide; NIH reviewers are explicitly cautioned not to follow applicant-controlled links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep necessary evidence and explanation inside the grant pages. The post stresses: "DO. NOT. EXPECT. REVIEWERS. TO. READ. YOUR. BLOG! ...or your papers." Also: "NIH reviewers are explicitly cautioned not to follow links to sites controlled by the applicant."

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the proposal self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey a convincing and understandable message within the confines of the page limit so reviewers do not have to hunt for information elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice repeated in comments: "convey a convincing and understandable message within the confines of the page limit because not everyone is an expert" and "People read your grants because they have to. Don't make them work for it."

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide the reader through the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure and narrative should draw the reader through the proposal "by the hand," providing clear signposting and logical flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit phrasing from the post: "Draw the reader through it by the hand." Use clear transitions, explicit statements of aims/hypotheses, and stepwise logic so reviewers can follow easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct and avoid verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good applications are usually succinct; avoid excessive length that may invite criticism or misreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal recommendations include not exceeding ~10 pages (one commenter) and the general admonition "Good applications are usually succinct and not verbose." Balance brevity with necessary explanation for non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insult reviewers; maintain professional tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid condescending or insulting language toward reviewers or readers; clarity can be achieved without being insulting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters criticize tone: "one can be clear without insulting anyone's intelligence" and warn that an insulting tone can provoke negative reactions and may harm future reviews. Keep a calm, explanatory voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize extra work for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid forcing reviewers to do extra work (e.g., chase down citations, re-figure methods) because annoyed reviewers may penalize the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated aphorism: "Don't 'annoy' the reviewers by making them do 'extra work.'" Make data, methods, and rationale straightforward and easily assessable within the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly address controversies and alternative interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: When literature has conflicting conclusions, explicitly acknowledge and discuss alternative interpretations so reviewers don't dismiss your proposal because of perceived oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes that if there are papers pointing in different directions you should explain why you interpret them one way; otherwise reviewers may think you ignored contradictory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe methods and technical details clearly and accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure methods proposed are clearly described to prevent factual errors or reviewer confusion about what you actually proposed to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the post: reviewer criticized a method that wasn't proposed and suggested a method that was already in the proposal; to avoid this, include clear methods text and figures with citations. When basic techniques are relevant, include sufficient explanation without being patronizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid including applicant-controlled external links
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on links to blogs or applicant-controlled material to communicate key information; NIH discourages reviewers from following such links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes: "NIH reviewers are explicitly cautioned not to follow links to sites controlled by the applicant." Keep essential content inside the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet grants with experienced colleagues/mentors before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Have experienced colleagues or mentors review your proposal pre-submission to catch clarity problems, assumptions, or tone issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recommend getting an experienced colleague to read proposals; one anecdote: "I wonder if this person had an experienced colleague/mentor at their institution look at this proposal before it went in." Use mock reviews and senior feedback to anticipate reviewer reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent and accurate in publication lists/CVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate abstracts, reviews, and non–peer-reviewed items from peer-reviewed research publications to avoid misrepresenting productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters: "separate abstracts from real peer reviewed papers, and reviews from research papers" and "Not doing so will put off a lot of people." Keep publications lists clear about item types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume responsibility for communication errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Default to the view that misunderstandings are often the applicant's fault (unclear communication) rather than reviewer incompetence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post states: "The basic assumption should be that information transmission errors are the responsibility of the sender, not the receiver." Use that mindset to improve clarity and reduce complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer professionalism: avoid funding statements and inflammatory language
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be dispassionate, avoid funding-outcome statements (e.g., 'in no case fundable'), and refrain from editorializing or inflammatory punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter noted that a phrase like "in no case fundable" violates NIH aims to separate review from funding, and that exclamation points and snide remarks are unhelpful. SROs should edit out unprofessional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recusal and appropriate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should recuse themselves when they lack requisite expertise for aspects of a proposal; panels should aim to match applications with appropriate expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters: reviewers often review outside their expertise; SROs still invite them. The rubric: have appropriate expertise or recuse. Program officers and CSR/SROs should strive to assemble panels with adequate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider appeal selectively but recognize limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may consider appealing reviews that contain clear factual errors, particularly if an A1 and the Program Officer supports an appeal, but the appeal process is often ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter: "in this case one should consider appeal, especially if an A1 and your PO is on your side." Multiple comments caution that appeals are rarely successful in practice (NOT-OD-11-064 referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective quotation and misuse of applicant's prior work in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not cherry-pick or selectively quote applicant publications to build a negative narrative; critiques should fairly represent the applicant's record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants report reviewers selectively quoting or omitting information from papers to support a take-down. Reviewers should be asked to represent prior work accurately and contextually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel scoring/resolution: allow sufficient discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Review and scoring systems should permit sufficient discrimination (more than coarse integers) so grants can be properly ranked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters lamented limited scoring granularity (e.g., only 3 digits or few integers for discussed grants) and suggested allowing finer-scale scoring to reduce ties and subjective clustering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality and guard against misuse of proposal content
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant systems must maintain confidentiality (CDAs) to prevent reviewers from misusing proprietary application information; applicants should be aware of policies and possible recourse for breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote in the comments describes suspected misuse of proposal ideas by a reviewer/colleague; commenters reference confidentiality agreements and potential NIH/OIG reporting routes for suspected misuse.
